questions.q: What does MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) actually measure?
options: The gap between when an attack started and when the SOC first noticed it
The gap between detection and the incident being fully resolved
The total number of alerts fired in a given shift
The average time an analyst spends writing a case note
questions.explain: MTTD measures attacker dwell time — how long the attack ran before anyone in the SOC became aware of it.

questions.q: What does MTTR (Mean Time to Respond/Resolve) measure, and how is it different from MTTD?
options: The gap from detection to containment or resolution — MTTD measures awareness, MTTR measures action
The exact same thing as MTTD, just under a different name
How long it takes to write the final incident report
The number of analysts assigned to a single incident
questions.explain: MTTD is about noticing the attack; MTTR is about what happens after — how fast the SOC actually contains or resolves it.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, the SIEM rule fires at 2:47 PM but log review shows the attacker's first malicious login at 1:15 PM. What is the MTTD for that incident?
options: 92 minutes
53 minutes
0 minutes, since the SIEM fired an alert
It cannot be calculated without the resolution time
questions.explain: MTTD is the detection timestamp minus the attack start timestamp: 2:47 PM minus 1:15 PM is 92 minutes.

questions.q: Why can a SOC have excellent MTTD but still have poor MTTR?
options: Because fast alerting doesn't guarantee fast containment — escalation delays or limited analyst access can slow the response
Because MTTD and MTTR are mathematically required to always move together
Because MTTR only applies to low-severity alerts
Because MTTD is measured in days while MTTR is measured in minutes
questions.explain: Detection and response are separate capabilities — alerting fast doesn't help if the process to actually act on the alert is slow.

questions.q: Why do SOCs track MTTD and MTTR as rolling averages over weeks or months instead of judging them by a single incident?
options: Because a single incident's time varies with attack complexity and staffing, so a trend line is what actually shows improvement
Because single-incident numbers are considered confidential and can't be reported
Because rolling averages are easier to calculate than individual timestamps
Because leadership only cares about the SOC's single best incident of the year
questions.explain: One incident's numbers are noisy; a sustained trend across weeks or months is what actually demonstrates the SOC is getting faster or slower.
